Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits gravitational-wave detector sensitivity; understanding coating anisotropy may help reduce noise.
method: The authors characterize silica films using techniques like ellipsometry and Brillouin light scattering to measure elastic and structural properties.
result: They find hidden anisotropy in silica films that resists standard heat treatment, affecting mechanical properties.
conclusion: The findings inform coating design and postprocessing strategies to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Colloquium: What Do We Mean By ‘active Matter’?
authors: Michael Te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, And Michael E. Cates
abstract:
Author(s): Michael te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, and Michael E. Cates

Active matter has become a lively topic in recent years, but what exactly is meant by the term ‘active matter’ is often unclear. This Colloquium discusses the scientific and semantic issues underlying this ambiguity, as well as the history of the field, and offers a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems. It then surveys recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 031001] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the definition and scope of active matter as a subset of nonequilibrium systems, including recent developments like quantum active matter.
motivation: The term 'active matter' is often used ambiguously; the paper aims to clarify its meaning and scope.
method: The authors review the history and current usage of the term, propose a definition, and survey recent developments.
result: They offer a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems and highlight emerging areas such as nonreciprocal interactions and quantum active matter.
conclusion: Active matter is a distinct field within nonequilibrium physics, but the paper does not present new results directly relevant to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and study molecular electronic and vibronic properties at the atomic scale.
method: Combines scanning probe microscopy with a nanoscale optical antenna at the tip apex to confine the electromagnetic field.
result: Achieves superresolution down to the atomic scale, enabling fluorescence imaging of individual molecules and submolecular structures.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy provides new insights into molecular identification and reactions at the atomic level.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review unifies the description of radiation forces and torques in optical and acoustic fields, focusing on momentum and spin densities.
motivation: Understanding how wave fields exert forces and torques on particles is fundamental for applications like optical trapping and acoustic manipulation.
method: The authors present a unified theoretical framework based on local energy, momentum, and spin densities in both optical and acoustic waves.
result: They show that the same physical principles govern forces and torques in optics and acoustics, enabling cross-disciplinary insights.
conclusion: The unified perspective can guide future developments in particle manipulation and wave-matter interactions.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements
authors: Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, And Thomas E. Albrecht
abstract:
Author(s): Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, and Thomas E. Albrecht

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of the physics and chemistry of transplutonium elements under high pressure, focusing on their electronic properties and material behavior.
motivation: Transplutonium elements are important for nuclear applications and exhibit unique electronic behavior at the boundary between localized and itinerant 5f electrons.
method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical studies of transplutonium metals, alloys, and coordination complexes under high pressure.
result: It summarizes the current understanding of pressure-induced changes in electronic structure, bonding, and phase transitions in these materials.
conclusion: The review highlights the challenges and advances in studying transplutonium compounds, but does not directly contribute to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and the multimessenger implications.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper reviews detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and emphasizes simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It surveys potential implications for understanding physical and astrophysical processes in dense neutron star environments.
conclusion: Multimessenger observations combining gravitational and electromagnetic data will enhance our understanding of neutron star interiors and related physics.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:
Author(s): Geoffrey Hinton

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: This is the Nobel lecture on Boltzmann machines, a classical machine learning model, with no direct connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: The lecture presents the development and significance of Boltzmann machines in machine learning.
method: The paper describes the architecture and learning algorithm of Boltzmann machines.
result: Boltzmann machines are a foundational model for unsupervised learning and have influenced deep learning.
conclusion: The work is important for machine learning but falls outside the specified research interests in quantum information theory.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers atomic-scale microscopy techniques for measuring disorder in semiconductors, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding atomic-scale disorder is crucial for semiconductor material properties, but the paper focuses on materials science rather than quantum information processing.
method: The authors review three real-space techniques: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, applied to compound semiconductors.
result: The review highlights how these techniques can be combined to characterize defects and disorder at the atomic scale.
conclusion: The paper is a materials science review with no relevance to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the quantum mechanical phenomena underlying low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, such as tunneling and resonances.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions at stellar energies is crucial for stellar burning and nucleosynthesis, but direct measurements are often impossible due to extremely small reaction rates.
method: The authors summarize the state-of-the-art theoretical framework for low-energy nuclear reactions, including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discuss new experimental approaches.
result: The review provides a comprehensive overview of the quantum physics governing stellar nuclear reactions and highlights recent theoretical and experimental advances.
conclusion: The paper concludes that continued development of quantum reaction theory and innovative experiments is essential to resolve open questions in nuclear astrophysics.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants based on a least-squares adjustment of all available data.
motivation: Accurate and consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology, and periodic updates incorporate new measurements and improve precision.
method: A least-squares adjustment is performed on a global dataset of measurements and theoretical calculations, taking into account correlations and uncertainties.
result: A self-consistent set of recommended values for fundamental constants and conversion factors is provided, with updated uncertainties.
conclusion: The 2022 CODATA values represent the best available estimates and serve as the standard reference for fundamental constants.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed for biological and clinical insight; optoacoustic imaging offers high-resolution, deep-tissue optical contrast noninvasively.
method: The review discusses the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging millimeters to centimeters deep with high resolution, providing optical contrast in biological tissues.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical imaging, with ongoing developments in multimodal approaches.

title: Progenitor Of The Recoiling Supermassive Black Hole Rbh-1 Identified Using Hst And Jwst Imaging
authors: Tousif Islam, Tejaswi Venumadhav, And Digvijay Wadekar
abstract:

Using a combination of Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope imaging, a runaway supermassive black hole was recently identified with an inferred velocity of [MATH], likely ejected from a compact star-forming galaxy at…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031404] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.

motivation: To understand the origin and dynamics of a candidate recoiling supermassive black hole.
method: Analysis of HST and JWST imaging data to locate the host galaxy and measure the black hole's velocity.
result: The progenitor galaxy is identified, and the black hole's high velocity is confirmed.
conclusion: The findings support the ejection scenario due to gravitational wave recoil.

title: Hidden Chiral Ferroelectricity In ${\mathrm{AgNbO}}_{3}$ Perovskite

abstract:

[MATH] is a lead-free perovskite with considerable potential for energy storage and optoelectronic applications, yet its low-temperature crystal structure has remained controversial. In this Letter, we revisit its low-energy structural landscape using a systematic first-principles st…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 036102] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates the low-temperature crystal structure of AgNbO3 perovskite using first-principles calculations, revealing hidden chiral ferroelectricity.
motivation: The low-temperature crystal structure of AgNbO3 has been controversial, and understanding it is important for its applications in energy storage and optoelectronics.
method: Systematic first-principles calculations were performed to explore the low-energy structural landscape of AgNbO3.
result: The study uncovers a hidden chiral ferroelectric phase in AgNbO3 at low temperatures.
conclusion: The findings resolve the structural controversy and reveal new ferroelectric properties in this lead-free perovskite.

title: Crust Glass Formation Reveals The Neutron Star Birth Properties In Igr J17480-2446
authors: D. A. Baiko And A. I. Chugunov
abstract:
Author(s): D. A. Baiko and A. I. Chugunov

IGR J17480-2446 is a low-mass x-ray binary, harboring an exceptional accreting pulsar (a neutron star) with an unusual spin frequency of 11 Hz and a very slow postoutburst crust cooling. The former may imply that it is observed at an early stage of recycling, while the latter was shown to indicate t…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031402] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies crust glass formation in a neutron star to infer its birth properties, focusing on astrophysical observations rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding the early evolution and recycling history of neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries.
method: Analysis of crust cooling and glass formation in the neutron star IGR J17480-2446 using theoretical models.
result: The slow postoutburst cooling is linked to crust glass formation, providing constraints on the neutron star's birth spin and age.
conclusion: The neutron star in IGR J17480-2446 is likely observed at an early stage of recycling, with a slow spin frequency consistent with its birth properties.

title: Anomaly In Canonical Semiclassical Gravity
authors: Viqar Husain And Irfan Javed
abstract:
Author(s): Viqar Husain and Irfan Javed

We show that the canonical formulation of the semiclassical Einstein equation, where the matter terms in the constraints are replaced by expectation values of the corresponding operators in quantum states, is inconsistent due to the nonclosure of the resulting constraint algebra.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031501] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: The paper shows an inconsistency in the canonical formulation of semiclassical gravity due to non-closure of the constraint algebra.
motivation: To check the consistency of semiclassical Einstein equations where matter terms are replaced by expectation values.
method: Canonical analysis of the constraint algebra in semiclassical gravity.
result: The constraint algebra does not close, indicating inconsistency.
conclusion: The canonical semiclassical Einstein equation is inconsistent.

title: Search For Sub-GeV Dark Particles In $η→{π}^{0}+\text{Invisible}$ Decay
authors: M. Ablikim et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): M. Ablikim et al. (BESIII Collaboration)

BESIII collaboration performs the first search for a sub-GeV dark scalar in →π0S decays using over 10 billion /ψ events, observing no signal.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031804] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: BESIII collaboration searches for a sub-GeV dark scalar in η→π^0+invisible decays using over 10 billion J/ψ events, finding no signal.
motivation: Dark matter particles with sub-GeV masses are not well constrained; this search targets a dark scalar mediator in a specific decay channel.
method: Analyze data from over 10 billion J/ψ events collected by BESIII, looking for missing energy in η→π^0+invisible decays.
result: No significant signal is observed, leading to upper limits on the branching fraction.
conclusion: The null result constrains dark scalar models in the sub-GeV mass range.

title: Dynamical Pathway To Radiative Divertor Driven By Transient X-Point Vortex In Tokamaks
authors: H. Yang, N. Fedorczak, G. Ciraolo, E. Serre, H. Bufferand, L. Fèvre, E. Havlickova, N. Lemoine, N. Rivals, P. Tamain, The WEST Team, And The WPTE Team
abstract:
Author(s): H. Yang, N. Fedorczak, G. Ciraolo, E. Serre, H. Bufferand, L. Fèvre, E. Havlickova, N. Lemoine, N. Rivals, P. Tamain, the WEST team, and the WPTE team

Recent X-point radiator (XPR) experiments in L-mode plasmas of the tungsten-W Environment in Steady-state Tokamak (WEST) tokamak show that a stable radiative ring can be sustained above the X point for approximately 70 s, on timescales not limited by intrinsic plasma physics, demonstrating the compa…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 035104] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies X-point radiator dynamics in tokamak plasmas, a topic in nuclear fusion plasma physics.
motivation: Understanding the formation and stability of radiative divertors is important for heat exhaust in fusion reactors.
method: Experimental observations and numerical simulations of L-mode plasmas in the WEST tokamak are used to analyze the X-point radiator phenomenon.
result: A stable radiative ring above the X-point is sustained for ~70 s, and a dynamical pathway involving transient X-point vortex is identified.
conclusion: The results demonstrate compatibility of X-point radiators with long-pulse operation, contributing to fusion reactor design.

title: Observation Of $cp$ Violation In ${B}^{0}→J/ψρ(770{)}^{0}$ Decays
authors: R. Aaij et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): R. Aaij et al. (LHCb Collaboration)

The LHCb collaboration has observed time-dependent P violation in a new hadronic
[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031803] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of CP violation in B0→J/ψρ(770)0 decays by the LHCb collaboration.
motivation: CP violation is a key phenomenon in particle physics that helps explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. Studying it in different decay channels tests the Standard Model.
method: The LHCb experiment analyzed proton-proton collision data to reconstruct B0→J/ψρ(770)0 decays and measured time-dependent CP-violating parameters.
result: CP violation is observed with a significance of 5.4 standard deviations, providing the first evidence in this decay mode.
conclusion: The result is consistent with Standard Model predictions and contributes to the understanding of CP violation in beauty meson decays.

title: First-Principles Explanation Of The Drift Configuration Dependence Of The Radial Electric Field And High-Confinement Access In Tokamaks
authors: B. J. Frei, R. Bilato, O. Grover, W. Zholobenko, C. Angioni, M. Bergmann, P. Ulbl, F. Jenko, And The ASDEX Upgrade Team
abstract:
Author(s): B. J. Frei, R. Bilato, O. Grover, W. Zholobenko, C. Angioni, M. Bergmann, P. Ulbl, F. Jenko, and the ASDEX Upgrade Team

The origin of the difference in the high-confinement ([MATH]-mode) power threshold between favorable and unfavorable drift configurations in tokamaks—experimentally linked to a deeper radial electric field ([MATH]) well in the former—remains unresolved. Using first-principles gyrokinetic simulations…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 035103] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses first-principles gyrokinetic simulations to explain the drift configuration dependence of the radial electric field and H-mode access in tokamaks.
motivation: The origin of the difference in H-mode power threshold between favorable and unfavorable drift configurations in tokamaks is unresolved, and understanding this is crucial for fusion reactor design.
method: First-principles gyrokinetic simulations are performed to model the radial electric field and turbulence in tokamak plasmas.
result: The simulations reproduce the experimentally observed deeper radial electric field well in the favorable drift configuration, explaining the lower H-mode power threshold.
conclusion: The drift configuration dependence of H-mode access is explained by the interplay of neoclassical and turbulent transport, providing a predictive capability for future devices.

title: Nonlocal Decoding Of Positional And Correlational Information During Development
authors: Alex Chen Yi Zhang, Pablo Mateu Hoyos, David Brückner, And Gašper Tkačik
abstract:
Author(s): Alex Chen Yi Zhang, Pablo Mateu Hoyos, David Brückner, and Gašper Tkačik

In many developmental systems, cells differentiate into a tissue by reading out morphogen concentration fields, a process fundamentally limited by noise. How much can the precision of this process be improved by nonlocal information, e.g., via cell-cell communication? Using a Bayes-optimal framework…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 038401] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how cells use nonlocal information to improve positional accuracy during development, using a Bayes-optimal framework.
motivation: Understanding how cells differentiate with limited positional information from morphogen gradients, and whether cell-cell communication can enhance precision.
method: A Bayes-optimal framework is used to analyze the improvement in positional accuracy when cells share information nonlocally.
result: Nonlocal decoding significantly improves positional accuracy beyond local readout of morphogen concentrations.
conclusion: Cell-cell communication can substantially enhance developmental precision, suggesting a role for nonlocal information processing in tissue patterning.

title: Hidden Sector Custodial Naturalness
authors: Thede de Boer, Manfred Lindner, And Andreas Trautner
abstract:
Author(s): Thede de Boer, Manfred Lindner, and Andreas Trautner

Custodial naturalness is a recently introduced idea that combines conformal and scalar sector custodial symmetry to address the electroweak (EW) scale hierarchy problem of the standard model (SM). We introduce a new model that realizes custodial naturalness without extension of the SM gauge group. T…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031801] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a model for electroweak naturalness using hidden sector custodial symmetry, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The electroweak scale hierarchy problem motivates new physics beyond the Standard Model.
method: The authors construct a model with hidden sector custodial symmetry to stabilize the Higgs mass without extending the SM gauge group.
result: The model provides a viable mechanism for custodial naturalness.
conclusion: The paper presents a new approach to the hierarchy problem but is outside the scope of quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Study Of The Reactions $\overline{n}p→2{π}^{+}{π}^{−}$, $2{π}^{+}{π}^{−}{π}^{0}$, And $2{π}^{+}{π}^{−}2{π}^{0}$ Using $J/ψ→p{π}^{−}\overline{n}$

tldr: This paper reports experimental measurements of antineutron-proton annihilation reactions using BESIII detector data.
motivation: To study the dynamics of antinucleon-nucleon annihilation and test theoretical models of strong interactions.
method: Analysis of J/ψ decays to pπ⁻n̄ events collected at BEPCII, reconstructing final states with multiple pions.
result: Measured cross sections and angular distributions for the reactions n̄p → 2π⁺π⁻, 2π⁺π⁻π⁰, and 2π⁺π⁻2π⁰.

title: Significance Of Microtearing Turbulence In Turbulence-Reduced High-Density-Gradient Plasmas In Wendelstein 7-x
authors: H. Cu-Castillo, A. Bañón Navarro, G. Merlo, F. Reimold, T. Romba, O. Ford, S. Bannmann, L. Vanó, M. Wappl, J. Geiger, A. Goodman, A. Zocco, F. Jenko, And W7-X Team
abstract:
Author(s): H. Cu-Castillo, A. Bañón Navarro, G. Merlo, F. Reimold, T. Romba, O. Ford, S. Bannmann, L. Vanó, M. Wappl, J. Geiger, A. Goodman, A. Zocco, F. Jenko, and W7-X Team

Gyrokinetic simulations of a turbulence-reduced Wendelstein 7-X discharge—characterized by a steep density gradient, moderate temperature gradients, and low plasma beta—show that microtearing mode (MTM) turbulence dominates transport. The simulated heat and particle fluxes agree with experimental me…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 035102] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies microtearing turbulence in a stellarator plasma, focusing on transport in fusion devices.
motivation: Understanding turbulence-driven transport in high-density-gradient plasmas is crucial for optimizing stellarator performance.
method: Gyrokinetic simulations are performed and compared with experimental measurements from the Wendelstein 7-X stellarator.
result: Microtearing mode turbulence dominates heat and particle transport, and simulations agree well with experimental data.
conclusion: Microtearing modes are a key transport mechanism in turbulence-reduced stellarator plasmas, informing future reactor design.

title: Deep Indentation Of Soft Thin Films Beyond The $10%$ Rule
authors: Huang Lu And Zhaohe Dai
abstract:
Author(s): Huang Lu and Zhaohe Dai

Indentation is one of the simplest ways to feel the stiffness of matter. Interpreting indentation, however, requires care, especially for thin films—such as biological cells or soft coatings supported by rigid substrates—because the substrate effect can make a film appear orders of magnitude stiffer…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 036201] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the mechanical indentation of soft thin films on rigid substrates, proposing a model beyond the 10% rule.
motivation: Interpreting indentation of thin films is complicated by substrate effects that can make films appear much stiffer; existing rules (e.g., 10% rule) are insufficient for soft films.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model and validate it with experiments to describe deep indentation of soft thin films, accounting for substrate stiffness and film thickness.
result: They derive a new scaling law that accurately predicts the indentation response for soft films beyond the traditional 10% depth limit.
conclusion: The work provides a practical guideline for mechanical characterization of soft thin films, improving interpretation of indentation data.

title: Two-body Fragmentation Dynamics Of Propylene Oxide Dications Induced By $112.5\text{−}\mathrm{keV}/\mathrm{u}\phantom{\rule{0.16em}{0ex}}{\mathrm{C}}^{5+}$ Impact
authors: Tuo Liu, Yue Gao, Shaofei Gu, Bo Yang, Hang Yuan, Mei Wang, Shaofeng Zhang, Xinwen Ma, Xiangjun Chen, Shenyue Xu, And Enliang Wang

motivation: Active colloids typically sediment or exhibit gyrotaxis, limiting their motion to 2D. The authors aim to achieve stable 3D transport for applications in microrobotics and material assembly.
method: Density matching and field-induced alignment are used to suppress sedimentation and gyrotaxis, allowing electrokinetically driven active colloids to move in the bulk.
result: Sustained three-dimensional transport of active colloids is achieved, overcoming previous limitations.
conclusion: The proposed technique enables 3D active matter transport, which could be useful for targeted delivery and microfluidic applications.

title: Dynamic Excitability Underlies Molluscan Shell Pigmentation
authors: P. S. Negi And E. Touber
abstract:
Author(s): P. S. Negi and E. Touber

Pigmentation in mollusc shells exhibits an exceedingly diverse range of patterns that raises questions on the mechanisms underlying such diversity. This work introduces a new class of excitable systems, which extends the well-known FitzHugh-Nagumo model to allow for dynamic variation of the phase sp…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033052] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper models molluscan shell pigmentation patterns using a novel excitable system extending the FitzHugh-Nagumo model.
motivation: To understand the mechanisms underlying the diverse pigmentation patterns in mollusc shells.
method: Introduces a new class of excitable systems with dynamic variation of the phase space, extending the FitzHugh-Nagumo model.
result: The model reproduces a wide range of observed shell patterns.
conclusion: Dynamic excitability can explain the diversity of molluscan shell pigmentation.

authors: Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, And Mahmoud I. Hussein

Author(s): Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, and Mahmoud I. Hussein

Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response well beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance, enabling broadband flow stabilization among other applications.

tldr: This paper introduces a concept called super-resonance that breaks the bandwidth limit of resonant modes and applies it to flow control.
motivation: Conventional resonance has a limited bandwidth, which restricts applications like flow stabilization. The authors aim to overcome this limitation.
method: The authors theoretically and experimentally demonstrate super-resonance, achieving a broadband out-of-phase response beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance.
result: Super-resonance enables broadband flow stabilization and other applications by maintaining a broadband out-of-phase response.
conclusion: Super-resonance breaks the bandwidth limit of resonant modes, offering new possibilities for flow control and other areas.

title: High-energy Emission From The Galactic Center
authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, and Régis Terrier

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy astrophysical emission from the Galactic Center, focusing on the supermassive black hole and surrounding structures.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength overview of the high-energy phenomena in the Galactic Center, which is the closest and best-studied galactic nucleus.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths, including X-rays, gamma rays, and radio, summarizing known sources and processes.
result: Describes the quiescent and flaring emission from Sgr A*, the presence of plasma bubbles and X-ray chimneys, and the complex molecular environment.
conclusion: The Galactic Center is a unique laboratory for studying high-energy astrophysical processes, with ongoing mysteries regarding particle acceleration and emission mechanisms.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: Searching for new hadrons and understanding charmonium decays provides insights into QCD, including quark confinement and gluon binding.
method: The paper reviews experimental results from BABAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII on hadron production in e+e- collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs.
result: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for high-precision measurements in this area, with recent advances highlighted.
conclusion: The review summarizes current progress and emphasizes the importance of ongoing experiments for validating QCD.

title: Editorial: A Tribute To The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Véronique van Elewyck And Dietrich Belitz
abstract:
Author(s): Véronique Van Elewyck and Dietrich Belitz

Three Colloquia honor the Arecibo Observatory’s legacy, exploring its revolutionary impact on planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.

[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 010001] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: An editorial tribute to the Arecibo Observatory, summarizing its legacy in planetary radar, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
motivation: To honor the Arecibo Observatory's contributions and impact on various scientific fields.
method: The paper is an editorial that reviews the observatory's achievements through three colloquia.
result: Highlights the observatory's revolutionary impact on planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has left a lasting legacy in multiple areas of science.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the scientific legacy of the planetary radar system at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on observations of solar system bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes the basics of planetary radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids and comets.
result: The Arecibo radar system was the most sensitive of its kind for over two decades, enabling detailed characterization of many solar system objects.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system made significant contributions to planetary science, and its loss marks the end of an era in ground-based planetary radar.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A historical review of the Arecibo radio telescope's contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To document the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory and its impact on various fields of astronomy.
method: Historical narrative and summary of key scientific achievements from the telescope's operation.
result: Arecibo made major contributions to pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave detection.
conclusion: The telescope's upgrades and longevity enabled a wide range of discoveries, cementing its place in astronomical history.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews advances in geospace science using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments.
motivation: To highlight the scientific contributions of the Arecibo Observatory in upper atmosphere and ionospheric physics.
method: The paper is a colloquium review summarizing key results from incoherent scatter radar, lidar, and optical measurements.
result: It covers advances in plasma physics, space weather, atomic metal layers, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory enabled unique observations of geospace phenomena, but the work is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The authors review experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of convection-cloud chambers that reproduce key cloud phenomena under controlled conditions.
result: Convection-cloud chambers can capture turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation, providing insights into the precipitation bottleneck.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales for understanding warm rain formation.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae, focusing on modeling and detection methods.
motivation: Core collapse supernovae are rare events that provide unique insights into stellar physics and multimessenger astronomy.
method: The paper summarizes recent progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection techniques in ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the current state of gravitational wave predictions from neutrino-driven core collapse supernovae and outlines methods for parameter estimation.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from a Galactic supernova would be a landmark event, enabling multimessenger studies of the supernova engine and neutron star formation.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on large-scale structure surveys.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole anisotropy in the distribution of radio galaxies and quasars with the cosmic microwave background dipole.
method: Analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in the matter distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may challenge the standard ΛCDM model, but further investigation of biases and systematics is needed.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: A review of astrophysical tests of self-interacting dark matter, focusing on dark matter halo dynamics and large-scale structure.
motivation: To understand the implications of self-interacting dark matter scenarios on galaxy formation and structure, and to summarize observational tests.
method: Review of theoretical models and comparison with astrophysical observations from galaxies to large-scale structures.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections from various astrophysical probes.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable model, with ongoing and future observations expected to provide tighter constraints.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for beyond Standard Model physics, but recent experimental results have constrained the parameter space, motivating a survey of remaining viable models and future discovery potential.
method: The authors survey current experimental constraints and theoretical developments, and project discovery potential across multiple search channels at the HL-LHC.
result: The review provides an overview of the status of supersymmetry and outlines the discovery potential of the HL-LHC for various supersymmetric scenarios.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable in certain regions of parameter space, and the HL-LHC will have significant discovery potential in the coming years.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion and neutrino production.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work from the last decade on nuclear reactions, plasma physics, and atomic physics in the solar interior.
result: It summarizes advances in nuclear physics of hydrogen burning and diagnostics like solar neutrinos and helioseismology.
conclusion: The review provides an updated model of the solar interior based on recent data and theory.

title: Nobel Lecture: Physics Is A Point Of View
authors: John J. Hopfield
abstract:
Author(s): John J. Hopfield

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030501] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Nobel lecture by John Hopfield reflecting on his scientific journey and the role of physics in understanding complex systems.
motivation: To share personal insights and perspectives on physics as a way of thinking, rather than presenting new research.
method: Narrative and reflective lecture based on the author's career and contributions.
result: No new technical results; the lecture is a retrospective on the development of neural networks and their connection to physics.
conclusion: Physics provides a valuable viewpoint for understanding complex systems, including biological and artificial intelligence.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding gas bubble dynamics is crucial for many natural and industrial processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The paper is a review summarizing key advances over the past 20 years in bubble dynamics, including experimental and theoretical studies.
result: It highlights the effects of turbulence, non-Newtonian rheology, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The review provides insights for modeling two-phase flows but has no relevance to quantum information theory or related fields.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in active matter systems, covering biological, smart materials, and robotics applications.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors.
method: Unified mathematical and conceptual framework, review of existing models.
result: Identifies a spectrum of behaviors from single-particle orbits to synchronized motion in dense assemblies.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter with potential for groundbreaking applications.

authors: Martine Ben Amar
abstract:
Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

tldr: This paper reviews nonlinear elasticity theory applied to buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding morphological instabilities in soft materials is important for materials science and biology, but the paper does not address quantum or information-theoretic aspects.
method: The review integrates techniques from nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, such as bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and elliptic integrals.
